text: Restaurants should be tracked as a system of franchisee unit economics, procurement scale, digital ordering/customer data, foodservice distribution, B2B beverage supply, kitchen equipment/service, and packaging regulation rather than only as consumer-facing brands.
Domino's remains the cleanest reference case for a restaurant franchisor whose vertically integrated supply-chain infrastructure may improve franchisee economics and support unit growth.

B2B coffee and beverage suppliers such as Farmer Brothers and Westrock Coffee are high-priority underfollowed lanes because private-label and foodservice relationships can hide behind visible restaurant brands.

Restaurant technology platforms, including ordering, POS, loyalty, and aggregator integration, should be researched as potential control points over customer data, transaction flow, and franchisee operating efficiency.

Commercial kitchen equipment, refrigeration, beverage equipment, and service networks remain plausible second-order beneficiaries from restaurant openings, remodels, automation, labor substitution, and maintenance needs.

Layer 2 must add primary-source verification, market-pricing checks, analyst coverage, leverage, customer concentration, and revenue-mix data before any candidate can be upgraded from Layer 1 relevance to validated thesis status.

The current restaurant universe is still narrow outside U.S.-listed names and needs additional global master franchisees, foodservice suppliers, packaging companies, equipment/service companies, and regional restaurant operators.

For Restaurants, do not start with only branded restaurant operators. Track the chain as: consumer traffic -> franchisee economics -> food/paper/beverage inputs -> distributor/procurement channels -> forecasting and supplier coordination -> POS/order/loyalty software -> delivery economics -> kitchen equipment/service -> packaging/regulatory gates.
Foodservice distribution concentration and independent restaurant procurement dependency are likely higher-quality bottleneck nodes than most brand-level restaurant narratives.
Supplier coordination, store-level forecasting, and inventory/order-management tools are hidden chokepoints because poor execution creates both stockouts and waste.

Franchisee unit economics are the main capacity gate for franchised restaurant systems; track food and paper, labor, occupancy, remodel capex, delivery mix, royalties, closure rates, and development commitments.
B2B coffee, tea, extracts, energy-drink formulation, private-label beverage supply, and beverage equipment/service are underfollowed supplier nodes behind restaurant and cafe brands.

Restaurant software should be split into POS/back office, order routing, aggregator integration, loyalty/CRM, demand forecasting, and procurement/inventory coordination rather than treated as one generic SaaS bucket.
Watch for earnings commentary on stockouts, supplier fill rates, food and paper inflation, delivery commission pressure, loyalty mix, net unit growth, remodel costs, and distribution consolidation.

Need next-layer verification for public pure-play exposure in broadline distribution alternatives, regional distributors, GPO/procurement platforms, foodservice packaging, and equipment-service networks.

Need to verify whether OLO, PAR, MIDD, FARM, WEST, THS, and packaging suppliers have material restaurant-chain revenue exposure, durable customer contracts, margin expansion, and customer concentration risk.

DPZ should remain a reference benchmark rather than an underfollowed alpha candidate: its relevant Serenity nodes are vertically integrated restaurant distribution, franchisee unit economics, dough/commissary scale, and first-party ordering economics.

ARCO maps cleanly to the underfollowed emerging-market QSR franchisee/operator node; primary verification should focus on FX-adjusted growth, restaurant-level margin, unit development, remodel obligations, and McDonald's master franchise terms.

FARM is a speculative-shadow restaurant supplier candidate with possible B2B coffee, foodservice distribution, and coffee-machine service exposure, but survival requires customer/channel disclosure, liquidity, debt, and margin recovery checks.

WEST maps to the underfollowed custom beverage platform and B2B coffee/extracts node; the key chokepoint test is whether capacity and customer wins translate into profitable utilization rather than capital-intensive low-margin growth.

WEN is an underfollowed QSR franchise-economics test case versus larger QSR leaders; its relationship is currently a hypothesis until franchisee health, net unit growth, digital mix, supplier dependence, and remodel economics are checked.

THS remains a weak-evidence second-order candidate; its restaurant-theme link depends on proving material foodservice or restaurant-adjacent private-label exposure after the Farmer Brothers-related transaction.

RAVE is a micro-cap speculative-shadow franchisor with unusually pure small-franchise-system and supplier-incentive exposure; later layers must penalize liquidity, disclosure quality, franchisee closures, and governance risk.

OLO maps to the restaurant digital-ordering, aggregator integration, and customer-data node; the key evidence gap is whether it is mission-critical infrastructure with durable retention or replaceable middleware.

PAR maps to restaurant POS, loyalty, and back-office software; the key evidence gap is separating organic ARR, enterprise wins, retention, implementation cycles, payments economics, and acquisition-driven growth.
The candidate chunk was truncated after PAR, so Layer 2B relationships were mapped only for tickers visible in the supplied chunk: DPZ, ARCO, FARM, WEST, WEN, THS, RAVE, OLO, and PAR.

Market-pricing checks remain missing for all candidates: current market cap, EV/sales, EV/EBITDA, leverage, short interest, analyst count, liquidity, and relative growth expectations should be added before prioritizing Layer 3 work.

Software names OLO and PAR need primary-source verification on customer concentration, restaurant-chain penetration, ARR retention, implementation cycles, payments exposure, and gross margin structure.
B2B beverage and coffee suppliers FARM and WEST require direct customer/channel evidence because named restaurant relationships may be indirect, historical, private-label, or immaterial.

TOST mapped as the reference restaurant software/payments benchmark; relationship remains a hypothesis until latest filings confirm location growth, software attach, fintech monetization, retention, churn, and FCF durability.

SYY and USFD mapped as reference foodservice distributors for procurement scale, route density, private-label mix, case-volume trends, and independent restaurant health; require channel-mix and case-growth verification.

YUM, MCD, SBUX, CMG, and DRI mapped as reference restaurant operating/franchise systems, useful for benchmarking unit economics, traffic, loyalty, labor, food costs, procurement, and throughput rather than as underfollowed alpha candidates.

DIN, EAT, and BJRI mapped as underfollowed casual-dining candidates where the critical node is franchisee or store-level margin resilience under traffic, wage, commodity, remodel, leverage, and brand-cycle pressure.

Primary-source verification is still missing for most ticker-specific relationships in this chunk, especially TOST software economics, SYY/USFD restaurant-channel exposure, and DIN/EAT/BJRI restaurant-level margin durability.

Market-pricing checks remain incomplete for the chunk: market cap, EV/sales, EV/EBITDA, leverage, short interest, analyst count, liquidity, and recent relative performance should be added before Layer 3 prioritization.

SBUX has stronger external evidence than other reference brands due to the 2026 Reuters-sourced report on supply-chain issues, but company filings and management commentary are still needed to confirm remediation progress and financial impact.

LOCO maps to the underfollowed regional QSR/franchisee-health node; survival requires primary-source validation of same-store sales, restaurant margin, franchisee unit growth, chicken commodity sensitivity, remodel ROI, and regional concentration.

FWRG maps to the underfollowed daytime-dining growth-concept node; survival requires evidence on new-unit productivity, daypart economics, labor scheduling, restaurant margin, franchise mix, and commodity sensitivity.

GENK maps to the speculative small experiential-dining growth node; survival requires evidence on restaurant-level margin, beef-cost exposure, labor intensity, capex per store, new-market execution, and unit productivity.

NATH maps to the hybrid small-franchise/licensing node rather than a pure restaurant-traffic node; survival requires segment-level royalty, licensing, packaged-products, concentration, and capital-allocation evidence.

PBPB maps to the small sandwich franchising and turnaround unit-economics node; survival requires franchise pipeline, net unit growth, closures, margins, remodel economics, and labor/food inflation evidence.

SHAK maps to the mid-cap fast-casual benchmark node for premium demand, digital mix, restaurant-level margins, and new-unit productivity; it is less underfollowed but useful for comparing FWRG, GENK, PBPB, and CAVA.

CAVA should be retained as a reference benchmark, not an underfollowed alpha candidate, because attention is high and its main research role is comparing growth-concept unit economics, margin, cohort maturity, and market-pricing expectations.
Primary-source SEC filings and earnings transcripts are still needed for every ticker in this chunk before moving from Layer 2B relationship mapping to stronger Layer 3 thesis ranking.

Market-pricing checks remain missing for this chunk: market cap, EV/sales, EV/EBITDA, net debt, short interest, liquidity, analyst count, revenue growth, unit growth, margin trend, and valuation relative to growth and restaurant-level returns.
